notes: Wednesday 28 Oct 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Tue 27 Oct through early Wed 28 Oct (Taipei). Economy: SK Hynix record quarter; China markets lose $2.4tn; Fed expected to hold; Brazil markets crash after Lula win. Tech (USA): Amazon anti-tokenmaxxing memo; AI super PACs split; AI disinformation before midterms; CFTC probes Polymarket. Politics: Israel election too close to call; Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly flees to US; Oleshky truce; grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson. Literature (USA): ACOTAR midnight parties (hot); Bad Blood sales surge (hot); Jason Reynolds' Dig (hot); McCracken's Seven Stories About Tammy (hot). Social: Ebola passes 10,000 cases; famine warning for Sudan; UK £15m anti-misogyny fund; Egypt fines Lina Attalah, orders Mada Masr closed. Sources: The Guardian, BBC, CNBC, NPR, Publishers Weekly.

stories.headline: SK Hynix smashes records as AI memory chips sell like hot cakes
stories.dek: The South Korean chipmaker's sales passed 100 trillion won in one quarter for the first time, and it plans to hand about 100 trillion won back to shareholders.
stories.caveman: AI computers need two big things: a brain chip (like Nvidia's) and very fast memory chips sitting right next to it. SK Hynix, from South Korea, is one of the biggest makers of that special memory, called HBM. On Wednesday it said that in July-September its sales were 104.62 trillion won (about $79 billion), up 327.9% from a year ago. Operating profit was 83.33 trillion won, up 632.1%. Both beat what experts expected. The company plans to return about 100 trillion won to shareholders over time, through at least 30 trillion won in cash dividends and 60 trillion won in buying back and cancelling its own shares. It expects its newest memory, HBM4, to outsell the older HBM3E in the last three months of the year, and says 14 big customers have signed long deals covering more than half of what it can make in 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the other side of the AI boom: while some markets worry about an AI bubble, memory makers are earning record money. It is also why phones and laptops are getting pricier, because memory is in short supply.
stories.camps: Bulls: demand for AI memory is locked in with long contracts, so the good times may last. Cautious voices: chip industries go in boom-and-bust cycles, and huge profits depend on tech giants continuing to spend. Consumers: high memory prices are pushing up the cost of everyday gadgets.
stories.image_alt: SK Hynix signage at the company's office in Seongnam, South Korea

terms.explain: High-bandwidth memory: stacked memory chips that feed data very fast to AI processors.
Money a company makes from its main business after paying normal costs, before interest and taxes.
When a company buys its own shares, so each remaining share owns a bigger slice.
Cash a company pays out to its shareholders from its profits.
South Korea's currency.

stories.headline: China's stock markets lose about $2.4 trillion as AI fears bite
stories.dek: A tech index in Shanghai has dropped 40% since June, even though Beijing is pouring money into AI.
stories.caveman: China and the US are racing to lead in AI. China's government has put a lot of money into it, including a 60bn yuan state-backed fund that started investing this month, and it is betting big on robots. But Chinese stock markets have been falling hard. The STAR 50, an index of tech companies in Shanghai, has dropped 40% since June; other big-company indexes fell about 20%. Bloomberg says about $2.4tn has been wiped off Chinese stocks since May. AI stocks make up over 40% of the market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, so when they fall, everything shakes. Reasons: many tech firms don't make enough profit because Chinese shoppers are spending carefully; the US is raising interest rates; and the US keeps banning Chinese tech, such as humanoid robots, and may ban Chinese parts in data centres.
stories.why_it_matters: China is the world's second-biggest economy. If its AI push stumbles, it affects global trade, chip demand and the US-China rivalry, including Taiwan's place in the supply chain.
stories.camps: Beijing: keeps backing AI and robots as the future of its economy. Analysts: worry that weak consumer demand means the state-led model can't keep a boom going. US side: says bans on Chinese tech protect national security; critics say they also hurt trade and raise costs.
stories.image_alt: Humanoid robots working at a supermarket shelf in China
stories.image_credit: Photo: China News Service/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: An index tracking 50 big tech and innovation companies on Shanghai's STAR Market.
A number that tracks the prices of a group of stocks, to show how the market is doing.
When many investors sell at once and prices fall fast.
AI inside a physical body, like a robot, that can move and act in the real world.

stories.headline: The Fed is expected to hold rates this week, but may hint more hikes are coming
stories.dek: US inflation is 3.7%, and the Fed already raised rates in September. Chair Kevin Warsh doesn't like giving clues about the future.
stories.caveman: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is America's central bank. It raises interest rates to cool down rising prices (inflation), because higher rates make borrowing more expensive, so people and companies spend less. The Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September. Its decision comes out Wednesday (US time), and markets overwhelmingly expect no change this time. But prices are still climbing: the consumer price index rose 3.7% from a year earlier in September, pushed by soaring energy prices. Even without fuel and food, 'core' inflation was 2.6%, above the Fed's 2% goal. Meanwhile, mortgage rates above 7% are squeezing the housing market, and the job market is in a 'low-fire, low-hire' mode: few layoffs, but jobless people struggle to find work. Chair Kevin Warsh wants to move away from 'forward guidance', so investors will read every word for hints.
stories.why_it_matters: US interest rates move money around the whole world. Higher US rates can pull money out of places like Taiwan and weaken their currencies, as we've seen this month.
stories.camps: Inflation hawks: prices are still too high, so more hikes will be needed. Worriers about growth: more hikes could hurt home buyers and people looking for jobs. Warsh's approach: fewer signals and more reacting to the data; critics say this makes markets jumpier.
stories.image_alt: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at a news conference in Washington, DC

terms.explain: The US central bank, which sets the main interest rate.
When prices in general keep going up, so money buys less.
Inflation without food and energy, whose prices jump around a lot.
When a central bank raises interest rates.
When a central bank tells markets ahead of time where rates are likely to go.

stories.headline: Brazil's markets crash after Lula's surprise re-election
stories.dek: Stocks fell 13.9% in one day and the currency had its worst drop since 1999, as investors fear big spending.
stories.caveman: On Sunday, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil's left-wing president, won re-election, beating Flávio Bolsonaro, whom investors saw as more careful with government money. On Monday, Brazil's main stock index fell 13.9%, its worst day since COVID began, and the real (Brazil's money) fell nearly 8% against the dollar, its biggest drop since 1999. The interest rate on Brazil's 10-year government bonds jumped 2.46 percentage points to its highest in over a decade, and the Treasury cancelled two bond sales planned for this week. Lula promised popular things: protecting benefits, raising the minimum wage faster than prices, more housing and education help, tax cuts on basic food, and a 40-hour work week without pay cuts. Investors worry Brazil's debt will grow. Lula also faces a strongly right-wing Congress and an unfriendly White House.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a classic clash: voters want help with daily costs, while bond markets punish governments they think will borrow too much. How Lula handles it will affect millions of Brazilians.
stories.camps: Lula's supporters: the vote is a mandate for more social spending and help for working families. Investors: fear rising debt and higher interest rates. One analyst: expects Lula to calm markets first, then push for more spending room later.
stories.image_alt: Lula celebrates the election results in São Paulo

terms.explain: Brazil's currency.
The interest rate a government pays to borrow money. When investors worry, yields go up.
When a government sells new bonds to borrow money.
About government spending, taxes and debt.
Political side that usually favors more public services and help for workers.

stories.headline: Amazon tells engineers: stop 'tokenmaxxing' and use AI with judgment
stories.dek: A memo says counting how much AI people use is a 'deeply flawed' way to measure their work.
stories.caveman: AI coding tools charge by 'tokens', small chunks of text the AI reads and writes. Some workers have been 'tokenmaxxing': using AI as much as possible to look busy, without caring if the result is useful. Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard in May after finding people did this to climb the ranks. On Tuesday Amazon posted a memo, first shared inside the company in September, about how its software engineers should work with AI. It says things like token use, how fast teams adopt AI tools and the number of code changes are 'deeply flawed' measures that can raise costs and add complexity. They can still be used 'with care and judgment', but Amazon wants to judge long-term results. An Amazon engineering leader said they look at 'feature velocity', like how many successful launches teams make. Amazon says it has not put caps on token use. CEO Andy Jassy has said AI may shrink Amazon's office workforce in the next few years.
stories.why_it_matters: Companies are pushing workers to use AI, but AI bills are big. How bosses measure 'good' AI use will shape millions of jobs.
stories.camps: Amazon: AI will be at the centre of software work, but waste is not welcome. Workers: feel pressure to show they use AI, and some fear AI will replace jobs. Cost-watchers: other firms are capping token use or switching to cheaper open-source models.
stories.image_alt: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy speaks at a company event in New York

terms.explain: A small piece of text an AI model processes; AI services often charge per token.
Using as many AI tokens as possible to look productive, whatever the result.
A short written message sent inside an organisation.
An AI model whose code or weights are shared publicly, often cheaper to run.

stories.headline: Silicon Valley's AI money splits in two ahead of the midterms
stories.dek: Groups wanting faster AI with lighter rules have spent about $8m on House and Senate races, vs about $6.9m from groups wanting stronger safeguards.
stories.caveman: In US elections, 'super PACs' are groups that can spend unlimited money to help or hurt candidates. The tech world hoped to copy the crypto industry, whose super PACs spent over $130m in 2024 and backed winners in 53 of 58 races. So in August 2025, Leading the Future launched with more than $100m in commitments from tech names like Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI president Greg Brockman, pushing for faster AI growth and one set of national rules. But another camp wants stronger safety guardrails and room for states to make their own rules. A CNBC count of federal filings shows the pro-speed side has spent about $8m in general-election races for Congress, and the pro-safeguards side about $6.9m. In Florida's 25th district, they face off directly: one side backed Democrat Jared Moskowitz, the other backed Republican Scott Singer.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever wins more allies in Congress could shape US AI rules for years, affecting safety, jobs and the tech used around the world.
stories.camps: Pro-speed camp: too many rules, especially different rules in each state, would slow American innovation. Pro-safeguards camp: AI needs strong guardrails, and states should be able to act. Watchdogs: both sides agree on some regulation; the fight is over how much, and big money is flowing everywhere.
stories.image_alt: Protesters hold up signs reading 'Freeze AI now'

terms.explain: A US political group that can raise and spend unlimited money for or against candidates, but can't give directly to them.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, this year on Nov. 3.
Rules or limits meant to keep a technology safe.
Federal Election Commission: the US agency that tracks campaign money.

stories.headline: Experts warn AI-made lies are flooding social media before the US midterms
stories.dek: Platforms have cut their safety teams, and fake posts are cheap to make and easy to tweak.
stories.caveman: 'Disinformation' means false information spread on purpose to fool people. Experts told the Guardian that social media is full of an unprecedented flood of AI-made disinformation before November's elections, and many posts are 'slipping through the cracks'. After the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, Facebook and others hired big safety teams. But after a backlash from the right about free speech, Elon Musk buying Twitter (now X) and Trump's 2024 win, many of those teams were cut. Now platforms lean on AI to catch fake posts. Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen said you can now run a fake-news operation 'super, super cheap', changing a post slightly each time so some get past filters. One example: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico took time off with the flu, but a false story claimed he was in a mental-health facility in Ohio. His campaign showed video of him at home, yet the lie spread for days.
stories.why_it_matters: Voters need true information to make choices. If lies are cheap and fast, campaigns and voters struggle to know what's real.
stories.camps: Experts and campaigns: platforms must do more, and quickly. Platforms: Meta and X did not comment; YouTube said everyone follows the same rules. Free-speech advocates: worry that heavy moderation can silence real views, which is part of why companies pulled back.
stories.image_alt: People vote on the first day of early voting in New York City
stories.image_credit: Photo: Heather Khalifa/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: False information spread on purpose to mislead people.
When platforms check and remove posts that break their rules.
An insider who reveals wrongdoing at an organisation.
A firm that took data from millions of Facebook users for political ads, causing a 2018 scandal.

stories.headline: US regulator reopens probe into Polymarket, the election betting site
stories.dek: The CFTC is checking whether Polymarket broke a 2022 deal that banned American users from its offshore platform.
stories.caveman: Polymarket is a 'prediction market': people bet money on future events, like who will win an election. In 2022 it agreed with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the US agency that oversees this kind of trading, to block US users from its offshore site and paid a $1.4 million penalty. Now, according to a person familiar with the matter, the CFTC is investigating whether Polymarket broke that deal, looking at how it detected where users were and how it advertised in the US. It is also looking at Polymarket's new US platform, launched last December, including how it signs up and protects customers. This is part of a bigger probe that started earlier this year after a Wall Street Journal report said Polymarket paid creators to post videos of fake trades and fake wins. Polymarket declined to comment. The news comes one week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: Prediction markets have grown fast, and people can bet real money on elections. Mental health experts and lawmakers worry about gambling harm and fairness.
stories.camps: Regulators: rules must be followed, and customers protected. Polymarket and fans: say prediction markets give useful, real-time forecasts. Critics: say it's gambling dressed up as finance and can hurt vulnerable people.
stories.image_alt: Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan at the New York Stock Exchange

terms.explain: A platform where people bet on the outcome of future events.
Commodity Futures Trading Commission: the US agency overseeing futures and similar trading.
Based in another country, often to avoid a country's rules.
An agreement that ends a legal case, often with a payment.

stories.headline: Israel's election too close to call; exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc slightly behind
stories.dek: Turnout was the highest in decades, and Arab parties may win up to 18 seats, making them possible kingmakers.
stories.caveman: Israel's parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. To lead the government, a party needs friends adding up to 61. On Tuesday Israelis voted in huge numbers, with a record turnout among Arab citizens. Exit polls (quick surveys of voters as they leave polling stations, not final results) suggested the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief, would win slightly more seats than Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right and far-right coalition. Netanyahu's Likud still looked like the single biggest party. Arab parties might win up to 18 seats. Eisenkot said before the vote that he would not form a government with them, so neither side has an easy path to a majority. That could mean weeks of deal-making, or even another election; meanwhile Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker. Final counting continues.
stories.why_it_matters: Israel's government shapes the wars in Gaza and the wider region. A change in leadership could change policy on peace talks, Iran and Palestinians.
stories.camps: Opposition: says the result is a rejection of Netanyahu. Netanyahu's camp: Likud remains the biggest party, and a stalemate could keep him in power. Arab parties: their strong showing gives Arab citizens more voice, though some Jewish parties refuse to govern with them.
stories.image_alt: Members of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party react to the exit polls
stories.image_credit: Photo: Amir Levy/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Israel's parliament, with 120 seats.
A survey of voters as they leave polling stations, used to predict results early.
A group of parties that join together to form a government.
A smaller group whose support decides who gets power.
A government that stays on temporarily until a new one is formed.

stories.headline: Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly flees to the US after losing to Lula
stories.dek: Lula called it 'shameful'; Bolsonaro missed a deadline to hand in his passport, and the US says it will give his family visas.
stories.caveman: Flávio Bolsonaro, a far-right senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, lost Sunday's presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Brazilian media, including Metrópoles, Folha de S Paulo and CNN Brasil, reported that he flew to the US with his wife and two daughters, and allies said he planned to ask for political asylum in Florida. He had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to give his passport to federal police. A US State Department spokesperson said he and his family would get visas to enter the US. Lula, speaking at his 81st birthday event, said: 'He who owes nothing, fears nothing... The act of leaving Brazil is shameful.' Lawmakers from Lula's party asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro's arrest and to put him on Interpol's wanted list.
stories.why_it_matters: Leaders leaving a country after losing an election raises questions about the rule of law and democracy. It also adds to tension between Brazil and the Trump administration.
stories.camps: Lula's side: fleeing suggests Bolsonaro has something to hide, and he should face Brazilian justice. Bolsonaro's allies: frame it as escaping political persecution, which is why they mention asylum. US government: is letting the family in, which Brazil's left sees as political interference.
stories.image_alt: Flávio Bolsonaro speaks to the media in Rio de Janeiro
stories.image_credit: Photo: Lucas Neves/NurPhoto/Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: Protection a country gives to someone who fears persecution at home.
The most right-wing part of politics, often very nationalist.
An international request to find and arrest a wanted person.
An official document that lets you travel abroad; courts can take it to stop someone leaving.

stories.headline: Rare truce holds around Russian-occupied Oleshky as trapped civilians wait to be evacuated
stories.dek: The ceasefire, requested by Melania Trump, was widened across the Kherson region; Nordic leaders also spoke with Putin.
stories.caveman: Oleshky is a small city in southern Ukraine, controlled by Russia, across the Dnipro River from Ukrainian-held Kherson. Between 1,500 and 2,000 people there have lived under a full blockade: no food deliveries to shops since May, and some people are eating weeds. On Tuesday a local ceasefire began at 3am and appeared to hold; witnesses said the front line was quiet for the first time in four years. It is due to last until 11pm Sunday. US First Lady Melania Trump requested the humanitarian mission, and said it was widened 'within the Kherson region' to give convoys safe passage. Pope Leo, the UN and EU officials also called for a ceasefire. Buses are expected to take residents to Russian-occupied Crimea and Russia. Separately, Finland's president and Norway's prime minister had a 'frank' call with Vladimir Putin, linked to Russia-Ukraine-US talks expected in Abu Dhabi next month.
stories.why_it_matters: Even a small pause in fighting can save lives. It could also be a test of whether talks to end the war can go anywhere.
stories.camps: Supporters: any ceasefire that lets starving people out is good. Ukrainian observers: say the Kremlin wants to win favour with Trump and will use the evacuation for propaganda blaming Kyiv. Nordic leaders: say big differences with Putin remain.
stories.image_alt: A woman walks beneath anti-drone nets in Kherson during a local ceasefire
stories.image_credit: Photo: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: An agreement to stop fighting for a time.
Cutting off a place so food, goods and people can't get in or out.
Moving people out of a dangerous place to safety.
Controlled by a foreign army.
The Russian government (named after its headquarters in Moscow).

stories.headline: Grand jury refuses to charge Cassidy Hutchinson, who testified about Trump and January 6
stories.dek: It's another setback for the Justice Department's efforts to charge people seen as Trump's opponents.
stories.caveman: In the US, before some criminal cases go to trial, a 'grand jury' (a group of ordinary citizens) decides if there's enough evidence to charge someone. On Tuesday, a grand jury in Washington refused to charge Cassidy Hutchinson, according to two people who spoke to the AP. Hutchinson was an aide to Trump's chief of staff. In 2022 she gave dramatic testimony to a House committee about the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, when Trump supporters stormed Congress to stop the certification of his loss to Joe Biden. She said Trump wanted armed supporters let into his rally and refused to intervene as the crowd chanted 'Hang Mike Pence'. Trump denied much of her account, and Republican lawmakers accused her of lying under oath. The details of what prosecutors alleged were not clear. Grand juries rarely say no.
stories.why_it_matters: Grand juries almost always agree with prosecutors. When they refuse, it can signal that ordinary citizens doubt a case, here one many see as political payback.
stories.camps: Trump allies and some Republicans: say Hutchinson lied and should face charges. Critics: say the Justice Department is being used to punish Trump's opponents. Legal experts: the refusal is a sign of limits on that strategy.
stories.image_alt: Cassidy Hutchinson is sworn in before the House January 6 committee in 2022
stories.image_credit: Photo: Jacquelyn Martin/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: A group of citizens who decide whether there is enough evidence to formally charge someone.
To formally charge someone with a crime.
The 2021 attack on the US Capitol by Trump supporters trying to stop the 2020 election result being confirmed.
What a person says under oath, in court or before lawmakers.
The US government department in charge of federal law enforcement and prosecutions.

stories.headline: HOT: Fans party at midnight for Sarah J. Maas' new 'ACOTAR' book
stories.dek: A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in the hit romantasy series, came out Oct. 27.
stories.caveman: 'Romantasy' is a mix of romance and fantasy, and one of the hottest kinds of books in the US right now. Sarah J. Maas' series A Court of Thorns and Roses (fans call it ACOTAR) is among the most popular. Its sixth book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, came out on Tuesday, Oct. 27. The night before, thousands of fans went to big chain stores and small independent bookshops across the country for midnight release parties. At Politics and Prose in Washington, D.C., fans came in leather costumes, pointy faerie ears and sparkly tiaras. They played trivia, made friendship bracelets and got their faces painted with the colours of their favourite 'Court', a bit like picking your star sign. One fan said she could have just preordered online, but wanted to share the moment with other readers.
stories.why_it_matters: Romantasy has become a huge engine for book sales, helped by social media like BookTok. Release parties show books can still be a shared social event.
stories.camps: Fans: love the community and the escape these stories offer. Booksellers: midnight parties bring crowds and sales into stores. Critics: some say the genre is formulaic, but fans argue fun and big emotions are the point.
stories.image_alt: A fan gets her face painted at a midnight release party at Politics and Prose

terms.explain: A book genre that mixes romance and fantasy.
A Court of Thorns and Roses, Sarah J. Maas' bestselling fantasy series.
aliases: A Court of Thorns and Roses

terms.explain: An event held when a new book comes out, often at midnight.
An independent bookstore, not part of a big chain.

stories.headline: HOT AGAIN: 'Bad Blood' sales jump after a new Elizabeth Holmes documentary
stories.dek: Weekly paperback sales more than doubled after You Can See Everything hit cinemas.
stories.caveman: Bad Blood is a 2018 book by journalist John Carreyrou about Theranos, a Silicon Valley startup that claimed it could run many medical tests with a few drops of blood. It couldn't. Its founder, Elizabeth Holmes, was convicted of fraud in 2022 and sentenced to more than 11 years in prison; she says she is innocent. Now a nearly three-hour documentary, You Can See Everything, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, has become a surprise hit, earning $45 million in its first two weekends. It follows Holmes and her family in the weeks before she went to prison in 2023. After it came out on Oct. 16, Bad Blood sold 985 paperback copies in a week, up from 439 the week before, according to Circana BookScan. Sales this year are up 55% from the same time last year.
stories.why_it_matters: Movies and TV can bring old books back to life. It also shows the public is still fascinated by tech scandals and the people behind them.
stories.camps: Publishers: love the 'screen bump' that sends readers back to books. Viewers: are curious about Holmes as a person. Critics: some question giving a convicted fraudster more attention, while others say it helps people understand what went wrong.
stories.image_alt: The cover of Bad Blood beside the poster for the documentary You Can See Everything

terms.explain: A non-fiction film about real people and events.
A blood-testing startup once worth $9 billion that shut down in 2018 after its technology failed.
Tricking people, often to get their money.
A service that tracks how many print books are sold.

stories.headline: HOT: Jason Reynolds sells a new picture book, 'Dig', about a father and son
stories.dek: Illustrated by Taeeun Yoo, it comes out May 4, 2027, and was the first picture book Reynolds ever sold.
stories.caveman: Jason Reynolds is one of America's most loved writers for young people, known for books like Long Way Down, Ghost and Look Both Ways. He always wanted to write picture books (short illustrated books for small kids), and said he gave his publisher 20 to 30 picture-book ideas before he 'cracked the code'. Dig was the first one he sold, though another, There Was a Party for Langston, came out first in 2023. Dig follows a father and son who dig holes together everywhere, from sand to snow. In pictures by South Korean artist Taeeun Yoo, time passes and both grow older, until the father can no longer dig on his own. Publishers Weekly reports the book was inspired by the death of Reynolds' father in 2020. Atheneum/Caitlyn Dlouhy Books, part of Simon & Schuster, will publish it.
stories.why_it_matters: Picture books are often a child's first way to talk about big feelings like loss. A major author writing about grief could help many families.
stories.camps: Fans and teachers: Reynolds' books reach kids who don't usually see themselves in stories. Publishers: a big name helps picture books stand out. Parents: books about loss can be hard but helpful to read with kids.
stories.image_alt: Jason Reynolds, the cover of Dig and illustrator Taeeun Yoo

terms.explain: A short book for young children where pictures tell much of the story.
An artist who draws the pictures for a book.
A brand name a publisher uses for a group of books.
Deep sadness, especially after someone dies.

stories.headline: HOT: Elizabeth McCracken's tiny 'Seven Stories About Tammy' wins big praise
stories.dek: An NPR review says the 70-page book packs a whole family saga into seven linked stories.
stories.caveman: Elizabeth McCracken is an acclaimed American writer. Her new book, Seven Stories About Tammy, from the small press Biblioasis, is only 70 pages, about the size of a pamphlet. It is made of seven connected short stories about one family and their eldest son's girlfriend, later his wife, an older woman named Tammy. The stories first appeared in a literary magazine and in The Best American Short Stories 2025. An NPR reviewer compared it to the famous opening of the Pixar film Up, which shows a whole marriage in about four minutes: McCracken does the same for a family, using only words. The reviewer called the stories 'one brilliant piece of writing' and said the only downside is that the book is so small it is easy to misplace.
stories.why_it_matters: Not every story fits a novel or a single short story. Small, unusual books like this show how a writer can say a lot in very little space.
stories.camps: Critics: praise its emotional depth and clever form. Readers: may like a book you can finish in one sitting. Sceptics: some may feel 70 pages is light for the price, though fans say length isn't the point.
stories.image_alt: The cover of Seven Stories About Tammy

terms.explain: A piece of fiction much shorter than a novel.
Separate stories that share characters or a setting and add up to a bigger picture.
A small independent publisher.
A story that follows one family over many years.

stories.headline: Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases, the fastest-spreading in history
stories.dek: Nearly 5,000 people have died in the outbreak centred on Congo, and about a third of them are children.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a dangerous virus that spreads through body fluids and can cause bleeding and death. An outbreak declared in May, centred in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), has now infected more than 10,000 people, according to Congo's government. Aid workers say that is shockingly fast: at the same point in the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak, only about 4,000 people had been infected (that one ended with more than 28,000 cases). This outbreak covers the widest area ever, from Nigeria to Kenya. Nearly 5,000 people have died. About a third of the dead are children, and roughly three out of four infected children under 5 have died. The WHO's Africa director said, 'We must reach people earlier, bring safe care closer, and strengthen trust before fear becomes a barrier to survival.'
stories.why_it_matters: Diseases don't stop at borders. Fast outbreaks in poor areas need global money and help, which have been cut in recent years.
stories.camps: Health agencies: call for faster care and more trust-building in communities. Aid groups: say they need more funding and staff on the ground. Communities: fear and distrust can stop sick people from seeking help, which is why trust matters.
stories.image_alt: A caregiver at an emergency nursery for Ebola orphans in Mongbwalu, Congo
stories.image_credit: Photo: Marie Ruwet/AFP via Getty Images (NPR)

terms.explain: A deadly virus spread through body fluids, causing fever and sometimes bleeding.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in one area.

stories.headline: 31 Western countries warn Sudan faces famine as the civil war drags on
stories.dek: About 19.5 million people, 41% of Sudan's population, don't have enough to eat.
stories.caveman: Sudan, in north-east Africa, has been in a civil war since April 2023 between the army and a powerful paramilitary group. The war has forced 14 million people from their homes. The US, the UK, EU countries, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, 31 countries in all, signed a joint statement warning of an 'alarming deterioration' in food security. They said fighting is the main cause of the hunger crisis, because it destroys roads, farms and markets, and they urged both sides to stop blocking humanitarian aid. The statement estimates 19.5 million people face high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million at emergency levels. An aid worker told the BBC that people returning to the city of Omdurman found their homes destroyed or looted: 'There is very little to survive on.'
stories.why_it_matters: Sudan is one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, but it gets far less attention than other wars. Famine can be prevented if aid can get in.
stories.camps: Western governments: both warring sides must let aid through. Aid groups: say help is badly underfunded and blocked on the ground. Critics: say statements aren't enough without pressure on the countries that arm the two sides.
stories.image_alt: A man and a boy holding empty bowls in Sudan

stories.headline: UK sets up a £15m fund to fight everyday misogyny as 'manosphere' worries grow
stories.dek: It is the first time the UK has had national money specifically to tackle sexism and hatred of women.
stories.caveman: Misogyny means hatred of, or prejudice against, women. The 'manosphere' is a group of online influencers who push anti-women ideas, especially to young men. The UK government said it will give £15m to a new misogyny prevention fund, led by women and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson. Groups can apply for money for things like mentoring young people, workplace training and awareness campaigns to make women and girls safer. Ministers also hope companies and rich donors will add money. Past campaigns praised include London transport posters that encouraged men to speak up when they see a friend behaving abusively. 'Day to day misogyny – from sexist slurs and harassment to workplace discrimination – quite simply has no place in modern Britain,' Phillipson said. The chancellor's budget is on Wednesday.
stories.why_it_matters: Online hate can shape how boys and young men see women. Prevention and education aim to stop harassment and violence before they start.
stories.camps: Government: prevention is key, and it is 'putting its money where its mouth is'. Supporters: welcome national funding for the first time. Critics: some say awareness campaigns have done little to stop serious violence against women, and £15m is small.

stories.headline: Egypt court fines editor Lina Attalah and orders independent news site Mada Masr closed
stories.dek: Amnesty called it 'a crushing blow to press freedom'; Egypt is among the world's top jailers of journalists.
stories.caveman: Mada Masr is one of the few independent news websites in Egypt. A court convicted its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of running an unlicensed website, ordered the site closed and fined her 3m Egyptian pounds (about $53,500), the highest possible penalty. Her lawyers said she was held for several hours until the fine was paid. She rejected the charge. Weeks earlier, six journalists at a fact-checking site were charged with belonging to the banned Muslim Brotherhood. The Committee to Protect Journalists says Egypt has 25 journalists in jail. Rights groups say President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi has led an unprecedented crackdown on dissent since the military removed his predecessor in 2013.
stories.why_it_matters: A free press lets people know what their government is doing. Closing independent media leaves citizens with mostly state-approved news.
stories.camps: Press freedom groups: call the verdict an attack on independent journalism. Egyptian authorities: say media must follow licensing laws. Rights groups: see it as part of a wider crackdown on critics.
